lessons.title: Markov Switching Autoregression for Volatility Modeling

body.text: Volatility clusters, large moves follow large moves, but the degree of clustering itself changes by regime. A single volatility model fit once over the whole sample misses that the clustering in a panic can decay at a completely different rate than the clustering in a calm market.

children.text: Chapter 1 and 2 treated volatility as a level: high or low, calm or extreme. This lesson treats it as a process with its own dynamics, how strongly today's volatility depends on yesterday's, and shows why those dynamics themselves deserve to be regime-dependent.
GARCH: The Standard Way to Model Volatility Persistence

The standard tool for modeling volatility persistence is GARCH, short for Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity, introduced by Tim Bollerslev in 1986 and still the workhorse of volatility modeling across finance.

body.caption: GARCH(1,1): today's variance depends on yesterday's squared shock (alpha) and yesterday's variance (beta)

children.text: Alpha measures how strongly a fresh shock feeds into next period's variance; beta measures how much of the current variance level carries forward regardless. When alpha plus beta sits close to 1, as it often does when fitted on equity returns, volatility shocks are highly persistent: a spike takes a long time to fully fade.
The Limitation: One Set of Parameters for All Time

A single fitted GARCH(1,1) uses one omega, one alpha, and one beta for the entire sample. It assumes the same volatility dynamics governed a calm 2021 session and the worst week of March 2020. This is the same fixed-parameter assumption that broke every rule-based flag in Chapter 2, now showing up inside a more sophisticated model. A more careful question is not just whether volatility is high or low right now, but whether the way volatility behaves, how fast a shock fades, is itself different across regimes.
Why Full Markov Switching GARCH Is Harder Than It Looks

The obvious extension is to let omega, alpha, and beta each depend on the hidden state. This runs into a genuine technical obstacle: because GARCH variance at time t depends recursively on variance at t-1, and that in turn depended on the regime at t-1, and so on back to the start, the exact likelihood of a Markov switching GARCH model requires summing over every possible historical path of hidden states, a number that grows exponentially with the length of the series. This is known as the path-dependency problem, and it is why fully exact Markov switching GARCH is rarely used in practice; the literature instead relies on approximations, such as the one proposed by Gray in 1996.

body.text: This is not a detail to gloss over. A model that sounds like a simple extension, 'just let GARCH's parameters switch by regime,' turns out to require serious approximation machinery to even estimate. This course does not implement full Markov switching GARCH for exactly that reason, and uses a more tractable alternative instead.

children.text: The Practical Approach This Course Uses

Instead of a fully specified Markov switching GARCH, apply Lesson 1's Markov switching autoregression directly to a volatility proxy, such as the log of realized variance, rather than to returns themselves. This sidesteps GARCH's recursive path-dependency problem entirely, because the autoregression here is on the volatility proxy series directly, not on a variance equation that recursively depends on its own regime-conditional past.

body.caption: Three ways to model regime-dependent volatility persistence

cells: No, one set of dynamics for the whole sample
Hard: the path-dependency problem, needs approximations like Gray (1996)
MS-AR on a volatility proxy (this course)
Level and persistence per regime, on log realized variance
Yes, both level and persistence are regime-dependent

children.text: Reading Persistence in a Volatility Proxy

Suppose fitting this model on Nifty data produces a calm-state phi of 0.30 and a stressed-state phi of 0.85. A useful way to translate phi into something intuitive is the shock half-life, the number of periods it takes a volatility shock's effect to decay by half.

body.caption: Number of periods for a shock's effect to decay by half, given persistence phi

body.label: Illustrative volatility shock half-life
body.context: ln(0.5)/ln(0.30) ≈ 0.58 for calm, ln(0.5)/ln(0.85) ≈ 4.27 for stressed. A volatility shock that fades within a single calm day can take more than 4 days to fade once the market is in the stressed regime, over 7 times longer, even before accounting for the stressed regime's higher variance level in the first place.

body.text: This is the concrete payoff of letting phi switch by regime rather than treating volatility persistence as fixed: a risk model that assumes calm-regime decay speeds during a stressed period will underestimate how long elevated volatility is likely to stick around, exactly the kind of mistake Chapter 8's risk management is built to catch.

body.title: Computing a Shock Half-Life
body.prompt: An elevated volatility state has a fitted persistence of phi = 0.60. Using half-life = ln(0.5) / ln(phi), what is the shock half-life in days?
body.explanation: half-life = ln(0.5) / ln(0.60) = (-0.6931) / (-0.5108) ≈ 1.36 days. This sits between the calm state's roughly 0.58-day half-life and the stressed state's roughly 4.27-day half-life, exactly where you would expect an intermediate regime's persistence to fall.

body.title: Why This Course Avoids Full MS-GARCH
body.question: Why does this lesson use a Markov switching autoregression on a volatility proxy instead of a fully specified Markov switching GARCH model?
options: Because GARCH itself is an outdated model no longer used in practice

Because full Markov switching GARCH's recursive variance equation creates a path-dependency problem that makes exact estimation require summing over exponentially many state histories, so it needs specialized approximations
Because GARCH cannot be applied to Indian market data
Because Markov switching models cannot be combined with any volatility model
body.explanation: GARCH's variance at time t depends on variance at t-1, which itself depended on the regime path up to that point. Letting the GARCH parameters switch by regime means the exact likelihood must account for every possible historical regime path, a genuine computational obstacle. Applying MS-AR directly to a volatility proxy series instead avoids this recursive dependency and stays within the same tractable estimation framework as Lesson 1.

points: GARCH(1,1) models volatility persistence with a single fixed alpha and beta across the entire sample, missing any regime-dependent change in how volatility behaves

A fully specified Markov switching GARCH is theoretically appealing but practically difficult, because its recursive variance equation creates a path-dependency problem requiring specialized approximations

This course sidesteps that problem by applying Markov switching autoregression directly to a volatility proxy, such as log realized variance, capturing both regime-dependent level and regime-dependent persistence
Shock half-life, ln(0.5) / ln(phi), translates an abstract persistence parameter into an intuitive number of days for a shock to decay by half

In this lesson's illustrative fit, a volatility shock fades in about half a day in the calm regime versus more than four days in the stressed regime, a difference with direct consequences for risk management in Chapter 8
